pr_title: Ensure EC keys with a private key but without a public key can be created
pr_body:
In 1.1.1 and earlier it was possible to create EC_KEYs that did not have the public key in it. We need to ensure that this continues to work in 3.0.

Fixes #12612

issue_context.title: OpenSSL 3.0.0-alpha6 6 Aug 2020 breaks perl Net::DNS::SEC ECDSA signature generation
issue_context.body:
The problem does not occur in the signing process itself.
This statement fails with an exception raised in checkerr():

  ```
	checkerr( EVP_DigestSignInit( ctx, NULL, md, NULL, pkey ) );

  ```
Returned value is 0, not 1 as expected.
Code works ok with alpha5 and all earlier releases.
I have not been following the daily snapshots, so unable to be more precise.

Problem occurs for both ECDSAP256SHA256 and ECDSAP384SHA384 signature generation.
Signature verification is not affected which should rule out problems with md.
comments: So, not being familiar with that perl module, please can you provide some kind of instructions to reproduce this? Or even better would be a standalone C based reproducer.

Matt,

Attached tarball contains a stripped-down version of Net::DNS::SEC with a
test file which consolidates all the active ingredients in one place.

cd /tmp
tar xvzf ossl_12612.tar.gz
cd ossl_12612
[edit recipe.sh to define path to openssl]
./recipe.sh

This will build the perl XS interface to libcrypto.so, run the test script
and hopefully fail in the same way as mine.
Note that the code which fails is common to all algorithms (except GOST).

Dick

Can you actually have any other key type without the public key? I do not see it being possible for RSA or DSA keys.
So IMO 2 should be doable and doing it just for EC keys should be sufficient.

> Can you actually have any other key type without the public key? I do not see it being possible for RSA or DSA keys.

Yeah...that's possibly true. I guess with EdDSA you might only have the private value.

It is difficult to provide any assurance that the private key is correct without also having the public key also.
I am not sure that allowing this is a good idea.

EdDSA signature generation does indeed use only the raw private key:
```
   EVP_PKEY_new_raw_private_key( nid, NULL, (unsigned char*) SvPVX(key) , SvCUR(key) );
```

Option 1 would be much the best IMHO.   Same EVP code will then work unmodified for 1.0.x, 1.1.x, 3.0.0, BoringSSL & LibreSSL.

Option 2 looks like wasted computational effort.  Public key is not mathematically essential for ECDSA signature generation.

Option 3 would mean fishing out the generator EC_POINT from the EC_GROUP in EC_KEY and a Montgomery multiplication using low-level APIs that the EVP stuff was designed to avoid.  This is even more wasteful than option 2.

Option [4] might be to reinstate the fortuitous bug in alpha5 until a better plan is hatched.

@romen any thoughts on this..
If you can reproduce the public key it doesnt sound like it is essential to have it.. That is not the case for other key types though.

An ECDSA key (as practised in DNSSEC) is a raw 256-bit or 384-bit integer.
The notion of "correctness" never arises.
The quality of the random integer is an entirely different topic.

Yes you are correct for the private key..
The key assurances apply to the verification part which uses the public key.

So this is all fine and dandy for ecdsa,
but probably not so good for ecdh where keypair validation is used.
So I guess it is possible that we could not have to have the public bit for that particular operation, but it does then mean that this would need to be checked for other operations.

>  So I guess it is possible that we could not have to have the public bit for that particular operation, but it does then mean that this would need to be checked for other operations.

Right. The key manager does not know what the key is eventually going to be used for. Indeed there is nothing stopping you from doing an ECDSA operation followed by an ECDH with the same key (whether that is wise is another question). So either you have to always generate the public part. Or always check everywhere that we use it, that it is actually present.

> (whether that is wise is another question).

The answer being that the key should never be used for multiple different purposes.

> The answer being that the key should never be used for multiple different purposes.

Of course. But from an API perspective there is nothing to stop you.
So this is sounding like a breaking change currently if we leave it as it is now?

> So this is sounding like a breaking change currently if we leave it as it is now?

It seems that way.

Personally, I favour the infer the public key approach. Yes, it potentially wastes some cycles that might end up not being used. But, hey, the user gave us a bad key. I think in most cases we should get a good key, and therefore there is no waste.
This is not just "a few cycles", but will be a very substantial performance hit.

When the key is generated you always compute both private and public keys, otherwise what would you give to the other party? So the computation was performed at some point. Why would you decide to not keep the public key does not make much sense to me. Maybe on some special device where the data memory is incredibly small it could be an optimization worth it but I am not sure OpenSSL as is (i.e. unpatched with some special hacks) is targetting such platforms.

On the other hand doing 1 would be possible but it would require extensive testing to ensure that we won't be crashing if someone imports a key with private key only and attempts an operation that requires public key.

I don't really consider (1) as a good way to go. Option (2) means we retain compatibility with a potential performance hit. The issue with this approach is that the user never gets to know that there was a problem with the key, and there is the potential for that performance hit to continue indefinitely every time the application reloads the same key. OTOH option (3) means that the problem can be fixed at source...at the cost of breaking some existing applications.
@romen your view on this topic would be appreciated.

So, I was under the impression that in general for EVP keys the assumption is that a valid EVP_PKEY object always has the public key part, and optionally the private key part.

This is reflected in most of the EVP code that in general does not check for NULL when looking at the public part of the key and considers a programmer error passing a key that was not fully initialized.

Unfortunately key formats that do not store the public part alongside the private part exist, and in those cases we are already computing the public part on decoding: we published [a paper about it](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01785) recently because unfortunately that code that handles these exceptional cases is not centralized so it can happen that we forget to apply countermeasures for SCA.

As the paper shows, for static keys, generating the public key every time one of these "weird" keys is encountered (and in this case it is even more complex because they are programmatically generated to not have the public counterpart), can be a problem as it gives an attacker a way to witness the computation of the same operation under the same static secret key, offering extra attack surface to infer more knowledge about the secret key using some side channel on the public key generation part.


In conclusion, my impression is that setting only the private key in a EVP_PKEY and then use it only on operations that never look at the public part works more by accident than by design in previous versions of openssl.
The same codebase that works for @rwfranks could be considered a programmer error the moment any other function would be called on that key object and looks for a public key.

> So, I was under the impression that in general for EVP keys the assumption is that a valid EVP_PKEY object always has the public key part, and optionally the private key part.

Yes. That is the case. It seems we have a case here where it just happens to work anyway.

> As the paper shows, for static keys, generating the public key every time one of these "weird" keys is encountered (and in this case it is even more complex because they are programmatically generated to not have the public counterpart), can be a problem as it gives an attacker a way to witness the computation of the same operation under the same static secret key, offering extra attack surface to infer more knowledge about the secret key using some side channel on the public key generation part.

So - that would suggest you don't favour option (2). What about options (1) and (3) above?

> So, I was under the impression that in general for EVP keys the assumption is that a valid EVP_PKEY object always has the public key part, and optionally the private key part.

Nope.  It may contain only domain (and other) parameters.

So, common combinations of components are:

-   Parameters
-   Parameters + public key
-   Parameters + public key + private key

(it's a common assumption that the private key contains the public key parts, so "public key + private key" is the same as "private key" in practice)

> Nope. It may contain only domain (and other) parameters.

Thanks for the clarification.

But never the private key without the public key (which is the issue here). Right?

>> 1. Relax the checks during import into the provider to allow this.
> Option 1 would be much the best IMHO. Same EVP code will then work unmodified for 1.0.x, 1.1.x, 3.0.0, BoringSSL & LibreSSL.

From the perspective of letting things work as they were (by accident or design), it make sense.
On the other hand, if a segfault happens because a function tried to access the public key part, happening inside the provider boundary I expect it will be harder for the programmers to debug the issue.

So, safer from a backward compatibility PoV, riskier from an usability and future developments point of view: if we keep it it might be good to reconsider our policy on not checking for invalid NULL arguments in internal functions. 

>> 2. Infer the public key if there is no private key during the import (if we go down this route do we have to do it for all key types??)
> Option 2 looks like wasted computational effort. Public key is not mathematically essential for ECDSA signature generation.

I am not against it, and actually I tend towards this solution from a usability and design point of view.
But we have to figure out how to do this properly (and I can have Triggerflow to addì this codepath among the things we test for regressions).
In particular while in general we have had to solve this problem when importing an "incomplete" key from some serialization format (and so we could put the extra code in the decoder), here it is possible to programmatically set the private key: one way to implement this is to check on set_private if the pub pointer has been set or not, and in that case do the extra computation.

>> 3. Just declare that you're not allowed to do that. This seems like it could break some code.

This is the hard line, I like it, but it's not the best for existing applications! 

> Option 3 would mean fishing out the generator EC_POINT from the EC_GROUP in EC_KEY and a Montgomery multiplication using low-level APIs that the EVP stuff was designed to avoid. This is even more wasteful than option 2.

The fix for this for static keys would be to use a serialization that does not throw away the public key, are there standards that mandate the encoding of the private key to not contain the public key?
The fix for ephemeral keys would be to do the keygen part via openssl instead of externally, because that way you are guaranteed to have both parts.

In both cases the user wouldn't need to reach down for the low level stuff.


> Option [4] might be to reinstate the fortuitous bug in alpha5 until a better plan is hatched.


This seems like a non solution: the internal legacy codepath is implicitly deprecated, and will go away as soon as the deprecated public API functions that still require it will be dropped.
It's only deferring when the breaking change will arrive, making the problem worse as we let more users adopt a pattern that works by accident but not by design.


----

In conclusion I would probably prefer solution 2, even with the caveats, but however we decide to go forward this seems to be breaking something for someone anyway, so maybe the OMC should be involved in deciding which breaking change to apply (or to go with 1 and somewhat avoid to take a stance on this)

> But never the private key without the public key (which is the issue here). Right?

That has never been fully explored.  Conceptually, it's perfectly possible to have a private key that truly only contains the private bits (for an RSA key, that's _d_ and _e_ at a minimum), it's just that no one has, to my knowledge, actually made such a key, presumably because it was never practical, and all standards (PKIX and so on) that I was aware of seemed to assume that the private key includes public key material (the new PKCS#8 version, I currently forget what RFC that is, extends the format to add the public key in an optional separate, so I assume that view is changing).

So, as far as I can remember, there has never been a sharp decision that an EVP_PKEY with a private key _must_ include the public key material, it's just what's been done in practice.

> 
> So, as far as I can remember, there has never been a sharp decision that an EVP_PKEY with a private key _must_ include the public key material, it's just what's been done in practice.

So could we suggest to go with 1, but add NULL checks everywhere the public key is used and raise proper errors instead of segfaults?

> So could we suggest to go with 1, but add NULL checks everywhere the public key is used and raise proper errors instead of segfaults?

Yikes. Sounds dangerous.
Option (5). Put a dummy public key in place. Any operation using it will fail, but it won't seg fault.

I think the root problem is that in developing the internals the assumption of "if it's not just parameters, a public key is present for sure, the private maybe" has been used most of the time in conjunction with the policy of not checking input arguments in internal functions.

Changing the assumption because it is de-facto not necessarily true anymore is what is dangerous, and the risk is compounded by the policy of not checking the arguments!

Uhm... 

> Option (5). Put a dummy public key in place. Any operation using it will fail, but it won't seg fault.

So I guess  a candidate would be to use "point at infinity" for a dummy public ec key...

It could work, but I see 2 problems:

- for other key types it might be difficult to define a "dummy" value for the pub key, as there might not be values that universally should deliver wrong results if used! 
- as we don't check input arguments and assume validity has been checked elsewhere than internal functions, it is possible that even in the presence of dummy values we compute a result, and then let the user use this result as if it was cryptographically secure because we did not raise an error: this can result in critical security vulnerabilities!

> for other key types it might be difficult to define a "dummy" value for the pub key, as there might not be values that universally should deliver wrong results if used!

I don't think we need to apply this technique to other key types. We only have to do it here because there is a specific backward compat problem that we're trying to work around. I don't think it should change our general approach.

> as we don't check input arguments and assume validity has been checked elsewhere than internal functions, it is possible that even in the presence of dummy values we compute a result, and then let the user use this result as if it was cryptographically secure because we did not raise an error: this can result in critical security vulnerabilities!

Hmm. Yes, good point. That would be bad.

It's also possible that this *was* considered in previous OpenSSL versions, and I simply glossed over that part.  That means the list of possible combinations needs being expanded:

We need to make a conceptual decision on this:
1) private must contain public
2) private need not contain public

We have docs and code that aren't in sync here. The doc is old. The behaviour has changed and sometimes 1) and other times 2).

Seen from a different angle, [RFC 5915](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc5915.txt) specifies the ASN.1 key format like this in chapter 3:

```
   ECPrivateKey ::= SEQUENCE {
     version        INTEGER { ecPrivkeyVer1(1) } (ecPrivkeyVer1),
     privateKey     OCTET STRING,
     parameters [0] ECParameters {{ NamedCurve }} OPTIONAL,
     publicKey  [1] BIT STRING OPTIONAL
   }
```

Do note the *optional* publickey.  This is the structure that we'll get from a PEM file with the header "-----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY-----".

So it seems that the rather stringent import of EC keys specifically actually violates this standard.

```
      specified in Section 2.2 of [RFC5480].  Though the ASN.1 indicates

```

Being stringent adheres to the SHOULD, which is generally speaking defensible.

Yeah, I (re?)discovered upon further research that both DH and DSA do exactly that, recalculate the public key.

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/bdde5b46c74852e38e660a16f64d7d8ba1c7c2e2/crypto/dh/dh_ameth.c#L163-L169

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/bdde5b46c74852e38e660a16f64d7d8ba1c7c2e2/crypto/dsa/dsa_ameth.c#L146-L151

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/bdde5b46c74852e38e660a16f64d7d8ba1c7c2e2/crypto/ec/ec_ameth.c#L208-L237

I'm really quite torn on this.  I find the public key recalculation ugly, and this also means that it must be reproduced in any decoder, which is an extra burden on whoever writes them (decoders having provider support means that anyone can write one for whatever data source they use), but I must admit that it meets the documentation.  On the other hand, there's nothing *conceptually* wrong with an EVP_PKEY with just the private parts and parameters...

This is a long thread and I'm not entirely sure what the root cause or solution is, but I'm just bringing it up now that, for EC keys, OpenSSL has always been tolerant to "private key with no public key" PEMs. The behavior we've seen in the past, is OpenSSL will compute and cache the public key when the PEM is parsed, whether the public half is needed or not. (Naturally -- there's no way for the lib to know what the application intends to do with the key after parsing.)

Also I understand that what a standard says about a PEM and how OpenSSL handles keys internally can be different -- which is fine, and does not in itself imply compliance/noncompliance.

In the context of ECC, when we brought this issue up with you in ... Aug 2019? Everyone seemed fine with that behavior -- e.g. compute public key immediately if it's missing when parsing the PEM.

OpenSSL is not alone in this strategy. We raised the same issue with BoringSSL, LibreSSL, and MbedTLS. All basically said "yea that's by design" with various reasoning, e.g. if you defer the computation until the public part might be needed, you can end up with a lot of duplicate computation across threads. (I don't know enough about the application layer to confirm or refute that.)

My team went through various other cryptosystems / formats as part of our [Certified SCA](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01785) paper. EdDSA was conceptually similar, but standards wise even worse because apparently they started with an ASN1 structure for private keys that did not support a public key field at all, that got evidently deployed, then the RFC finalized with a different structure, leading to nice [RFC 8410](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8410) wording like

```
   NOTE: There exist some private key import functions that have not
   picked up the new ASN.1 structure OneAsymmetricKey that is defined in
   [RFC7748].  This means that they will not accept a private key
   structure that contains the public key field.  This means a balancing
   act needs to be done between being able to do a consistency check on
   the key pair and widest ability to import the key.
```

After reading this thread, my vote does not count but I feel Option (2) is the way to go.

My team fuzzed so many libraries, so many different cryptosystems with various degrees of missing parameters. And various security implications of the results.

But in the wild we never found a private key that didn't also include the public key. (Unless the key format does not support it -- e.g. PVK DSA keys if I recall.)

So I feel like any "you're wasting cycles" arguments really don't have any teeth because such persisted keys, as far as our research told us, are rare at best.

I can't shed much light on the development history, but yes, as @levitte mentioned the field is optional in the standard encoding, and openssl is not the only library that computes the potentially missing public component at load time.

The reason why openssl (and forks) and other libraries do it is not really mentioned explicitly, but my understanding is that it seemed wise given that the library cannot possibly know in advance if after creation the object is going to be used for an operation that requires the public component or not.

Given that it was always possible to compute the public component from the private, that it is perfectly admissible that a user might want to compute a public key result when it only has been given an encoding without the optional public component from a third party keygen, it seemed more robust to generate the public component on missing at load time (which is usually already a slow operation anyway, and users tend to do load once, reuse many for static keys).
The alternatives would have been to do it "on demand", if a pub key result is needed from a key object missing the pub component, or to throw an error.

The latter can be seen by many users as a error, or missing functionality: all the information to compute the result is indeed available and there is no reason for the application/library not to perform the pubkey operation given a perfectly valid encoding of a key pair that omits the public component.

The "on demand" solution has several drawbacks, each with different priority depending on the hat you are wearing when thinking of them:

- from a API pov, a public key operation that is not keygen should never alter the key object in any of its components, so you either make the API non-`const` intentionally (and that opens another can of worms) or you can't cache the pub component for later reuses
-  generating the pub component from the private key and parameters is generally the most expensive operation of the whole cryptosystem (yes, it can be optimized somewhat for fixed generators and other assumptions, so there might be affine operations that are even slower, but bear with me) so you either trash the performance of applications by recomputing this and throwing it away if you can't cache it inside the key object or you trash the performance of the first such operation
- if you can't cache, repeating the operation that retrieves the public component from the private component, over and over, will give attackers a lot of ideal traces and it's a huge security risk for both sw and hw implementations


So... I tend to think that, although admissible because the standards say so, in general encodings that omit the public component are a potential risk, don't really have big benefits because storage and bandwidth is cheap (and this specific case is EC, so we are in the realm of very few bytes anyway, not huge FF keys), and that it is a good idea for libraries to ensure that their internal representation is always a key pair at load/init/keygen time and deal with keypairs or pub keys anywhere else than those critical sections.

One approach could be to still do the "compute pub component on load if missing" when decoding, and have only setters that take all components at once (e.g. `EVP_PKEY_set_keypair(pkey, priv, pub) `, where pub is optional and computed by the implementation if missing) and a separate purpose-built `EVP_PKEY_set_privateonly(pkey, priv) ` which creates objects that are intentionally created as private-only key objects.

> - How many people rely on that undocumented behaviour that
>   contradicted the documented behaviour, and is that enough to do

Unfortunately, there is no method of measuring how many installations of
Net::DNS::SEC were performed directly from CPAN.

The only end-users we get to know about are those who file bug reports or
suggest changes.  The more bugs that get squashed, the smaller that number
becomes.  Both ECCGOST and ECDSA were added in response to direct requests
from end users so at least some of them are doing interesting things.

The most prominent end user is Verisign's DNSSEC Analyser
<https://dnssec-debugger.verisignlabs.com/openssl.org> website.  Killing
off ECDSA in OpenSSL, even temporarily, will be a horribly public event.
Ed25519/Ed448 support was added specifically for that project.

All the enterprise grade Linux distributions carry Net::DNS and
Net::DNS::SEC in their repositories.
Again, there is no method of estimating the number of actual installations,
many of which will be within corporate networks.
Given the enormous size of the Linux installed base, and the number of DNS
admins worldwide, the impact is unlikely to be small enough to ignore.

> - If we do something about it, which of the various solutions
>   has the least potential to cause issues?

I would be happy with a modified version of
EVP_PKEY_new_raw_private_key(...) which works for ECDSA as well as EdDSA.
This would leave all the other OSSL APIs unchanged.

Doing something similar for EVP_PKEY_new_raw_public_key(...) would be an
added bonus, and would do the job entirely within the EVP orbit.  The
public key, in this case, would be a concatenated coordinate pair.  From an
end user pov, all the messy EC_KEY stuff then disappears completely.

OTC have voted that:

"For 3.0 EVP_PKEY keys all algorithm implementations that were usable with 1.1.1 EVP_PKEY API or low level APIs without public component must stay usable."

So we need to fix this.

review_comments: Did you notice the `include_private` further down, passed to `ec_key_fromdata()`?  That has lost its importance (I'm not sure why it was even important to begin with), so I'd throw that away, including removing that last `ec_key_fromdata()` argument.

Doesn't that mean that we would no longer pay any attention to the `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY` selection parameter? i.e. we would only drive things off of whether the private key data was actually present in the params - regardless of what `selection` says. That doesn't seem quite right to me....and if we no longer consider that selection parameter important, then perhaps a bigger refactor is required?

Saying that `selection` is unimportant if we don't specifically check for `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY` is a bit of an exaggeration, isn't it?  We do still check that a keypair is expected before calling `ec_key_fromdata()`, do we not?  However, I don't see the value with being that level of picky here if `ec_key_fromdata()` can discover on its own if there's a private key present in the data or not.

Frankly, I'm quite reluctant to make the suggested change. I seriously dislike the inconsistency of paying attention to some of the selection flags, but not others. To me that has a nasty smell about it. It also seems quite tangential to the point of this PR.
